summary: The completion-claiming path is small, deliberate, and — with one exception — sound in intent, but it has exactly one door: a run can only be recorded as finished if the model emits an explicit `done` for every task in a plan. There is no run status "failed"; `askme.py:4162-4187` shows the run loop producing only `complete`, `complete_unverified` (askme.py:2927, 4751-4752) or `exhausted` (askme.py:3840-3856), and `exhausted()` deliberately refuses any reconciliation to success (issue #68). The guards behave as documented — duplicate/stuck detection at `askme.py:3012-3208` suppresses a repeated action and, on the second consecutive strike, ends the attempt with a `[stuck_loop]` error, so repetition is never converted into acceptance. The gap the CI reds expose is not that the guards are wrong, but that nothing on the other side of them can say "the thing this task asks for already succeeded, here is the receipt." The only receipt-backed auto-completion in the codebase is the narrow #41 C-header repair (`_task_satisfied_by_deterministic_repair`, askme.py:2459), gated further at askme.py:3465. Suppressed steps are recorded only into the model's sliding window (`StepRecorder.note`, askme.py:2551-2554) and never into `all_steps`, so they are invisible to `_has_new_validation_evidence`, to `_write_visibility_flag` (askme.py:1730-1746), and to the final validator — a suppressed re-run can never supply the "new evidence" that a failed-validation recheck requires (askme.py:3746-3750, 3824-3834). A frozen bench record reproduces the full end-to-end failure with a landed, in-run-verified artifact: `tests/bench_records/2026-08-03/12b_easy/test_multi_step_build_trial1.jsonl` ends `run_end status=exhausted` after the compile succeeded twice. Two secondary defects are worth fixing before publication: the strike counter `dup_skip_count` is shared across unrelated guard types and only resets on a dispatched action (askme.py:2592, 4573), so one earlier rewrite-loop skip can make the very first duplicate shell/read kill the attempt with no corrective turn; and a harmless repeated *read* ends the attempt (askme.py:3171-3179) while a repeated *write* only escalates thinking (askme.py:3109-3112), which is backwards relative to actual risk and is precisely what produced run 135's `[stuck_loop] read ...` red. Finally, every coverage gap the parent listed lands inside this machinery — the aggregate 96.61% hides that the code deciding "is this run complete" is among the least-exercised in the repo.

findings.title: Only three terminal statuses exist; there is no run-level "failed"
findings.detail: askme.py:4162-4187 `_RunController.run()` loops `for replan in range(self.max_replans)`, calls `self.completion.try_finish(replan)` (4176) when `_execute_tasks` returns True, and falls through to `self.completion.exhausted()` (4180) otherwise. `RunOutcome.status` is documented as `"complete" | "complete_unverified" | "exhausted"` (askme.py:2927) and `COMPLETE_STATUSES = ("complete", "complete_unverified")` (askme.py:4751-4752). `task_failed` (askme.py:4312-4319) is a per-task JSONL event only and never becomes a run status. `complete_unverified` is produced at askme.py:3798-3812 when the validator is unavailable or malformed — deliberately not claiming "validation passed" from missing evidence. Public wording must therefore say runs end complete / complete_unverified / exhausted, never that a run "failed".
findings.next_step: Fix the vocabulary in any blog/README text: three statuses, and `exhausted` is the only non-completing one.

findings.title: An explicit model `done` is the ONLY general way a task is accepted
findings.detail: `_decide_step` routes `done` to `_handle_done` (askme.py:4546-4547). `_handle_done` (askme.py:4560-4568) consults `self.obligations.refuse_done(ctx)` then `self.step_policy.guard_done(ctx, attempt)`; if both pass it sets `attempt.done = True` and returns END_ATTEMPT. The default policy arm is `heuristic` (askme.py:537 `DEFAULT_STEP_POLICY = _validated_step_policy(os.environ.get("AGENT_STEP_POLICY", "heuristic"))`) whose base `guard_done` returns None (askme.py:2997-2999) — so in the default arm `done` is accepted whenever no incomplete-write obligation blocks it. The consequence is the whole issue: no `done`, no completed task, regardless of what actually landed on disk.
findings.next_step: Name this explicitly in the blog post as a design choice, and decide whether receipt-backed acceptance (finding below) is the fix.

findings.title: THE MISSING MECHANISM: no recorded evidence of a prior successful check can satisfy a verification task
findings.detail: Answering the question plainly: there is no such path. The single receipt-backed auto-completion is `_task_satisfied_by_deterministic_repair(task, state)` (askme.py:2459-2480+), called once at askme.py:4348, and it is triple-gated — the task text must contain "include" plus one of add/insert/edit/include/fix, the requested include must be `#include <stdio.h>` or `#include <string.h>`, and a prior step must carry the `deterministic_repair` flag. It is the #41 C-header ablation, nothing more. It is further refused when the policy arm has an open verification obligation (`allows_deterministic_completion`, askme.py:3465-3468, base at 3001-3006). `_deterministic_check` (askme.py:2185+) does inspect recorded shell/write history, but it is only reachable from run-level `_validate_completion` (askme.py:2244-2252) AFTER every task already completed — it can never rescue a task that failed. And `CompletionPolicy.exhausted()` (askme.py:3840-3856) documents that the former 'latest shell succeeded' reconciliation was removed on purpose. So the fix cannot live at the terminal; it has to live at task acceptance.
findings.next_step: Design a receipt-backed verification ledger keyed by (normalized target, normalized command) that `_handle_done` — or the path just before `task_failed` at askme.py:4309-4320 — may consult, using only `all_steps` receipts, never model assertions. Register it as a protocol change before any measured claim.

findings.title: Frozen record reproduces the whole 'work landed, run exhausted' chain end to end
findings.detail: tests/bench_records/2026-08-03/12b_easy/test_multi_step_build_trial1.jsonl: plan = ["Create main.c printing 'AGENT_OK' ...", 'Compile main.c using cc -o ...']; task 0 completes (`task_complete`) and its step 2 is shell `cc -o main main.c && ./main`; task 1 executes shell `cc -o main main.c` once, then emits `step_skipped reason=duplicate_shell`, then `step_skipped reason=stuck_shell_repeat`; a task-local replan rewrites the task to `gcc -o main main.c` and the identical cycle repeats; then `task_failed`, then a full replan whose planner returns nothing, then `run_end status=exhausted errors=['[stuck_loop] shell cc -o main main.c: same successful command repeated', '[stuck_loop] shell gcc -o main main.c: same successful command repeated', '[malformed_plan] planner returned no valid tasks']`. That the compile SUCCEEDED is proven by the code, not inferred: `duplicate_shell` is only emitted inside `if prev.get("ok"):` at askme.py:3113-3114. The binary was built and run; the harness reports exhausted. Many sibling records show the same `stuck_shell_repeat` on `cc -o main main.c` (2026-08-03/12b_medium, 2026-08-04/json/{easy,hard}, 2026-08-04/tools/easy).
findings.next_step: Use this exact record as the worked example in the blog post — it is frozen, dated, and self-contained.

findings.title: Guard asymmetry: a repeated harmless READ kills the attempt, a repeated WRITE only escalates thinking
findings.detail: Second consecutive identical successful shell -> `_StepFlow.END_ATTEMPT` with `[stuck_loop] shell ...: same successful command repeated` (askme.py:3119-3130). Second consecutive identical successful read (same `_read_key`) -> END_ATTEMPT with `[stuck_loop] read ...: same file read repeatedly` (askme.py:3170-3179). But a duplicate write/edit of the same target only sets `attempt.use_think = True` and returns NEXT_STEP (askme.py:3106-3112) — the attempt survives. So the cheapest, most harmless repetition (re-reading a file) is punished hardest, and the genuinely wasteful one (rewriting the same content) is not. This is exactly the shape of scheduled run 135's openrouter-smoke red: `test_create_and_read_file` -> status "exhausted" with `[stuck_loop] read ...: same file read repeatedly`.
findings.next_step: Consider making the read/shell second strike a corrective NEXT_STEP with a harder 'emit done or fail' note rather than END_ATTEMPT, and add a deterministic regression asserting the run still reaches `complete` when the artifact is correct. Do not change thresholds silently — this alters measured outcomes and needs a new protocol.

findings.title: `dup_skip_count` is one counter shared across unrelated guards, so an earlier skip can make the FIRST duplicate shell/read fatal
findings.detail: `dup_skip_count` is a single field on `TaskAttemptState` (askme.py:2592) incremented by the write/edit duplicate guard (3081), the shell duplicate guard (3119), the read duplicate guard (3170), the heuristic rewrite-loop guard (3299), and the lifecycle rewrite guard (3421). It is reset only in `_execute_step` (askme.py:4573, `attempt.dup_skip_count = 0  # reset on any non-skipped action`). Because the shell and read arms increment then immediately test `>= 2`, an attempt that already took one rewrite-loop skip enters the shell/read guard pre-armed: the very first duplicate shell or read then returns END_ATTEMPT with no corrective observation delivered to the model at all. Grep of tests/ found only `tests/test_agent_actions.py:1031 test_stuck_read_recorded_as_skipped` (asserting reasons == ['duplicate_read','stuck_read']) — the cross-guard priming case appears untested.
findings.next_step: Add a deterministic regression: rewrite-loop skip, then one duplicate successful shell, and assert the model still receives the corrective note instead of END_ATTEMPT. Then decide whether the counter should be per-guard-family.

findings.title: Suppressed steps enter the sliding window only — invisible to validation evidence, write visibility, and the final validator
findings.detail: `StepRecorder.note(entry)` appends only to `state["last_steps"]` and its docstring says so explicitly: 'Model-visible corrective observation: enters the sliding window only, never the run-wide structured record or the JSONL log' (askme.py:2551-2554). `StepRecorder.record` is the one that also appends to `all_steps` (askme.py:2556-2563). `StepRecorder.skip` (2539-2549) only bumps `skipped_steps` and emits a JSONL skip event. Three consequences, all on the completion path: (1) `_has_new_validation_evidence` scans `all_steps` for an ok write/edit/shell after `validated_step_count`, so once validation has explicitly failed (`mark_failed`, askme.py:3708-3711) a run that only re-runs an already-successful check can NEVER meet the recheck precondition at askme.py:3746-3750 and is refused at 3824-3834; (2) `_write_visibility_flag` (askme.py:1730-1746) reports `{"no_write_executed": True}` for a task whose only actions were suppressed; (3) the validator's evidence lines are built from `completed_step_groups` (askme.py:2255-2266), which suppressed steps never enter.
findings.next_step: If a receipt-backed verification ledger is built, source it from `all_steps` receipts only (never from `note` entries), and decide deliberately whether a suppressed-but-previously-successful command counts as 'new evidence' — the current answer is no, which is defensible but should be a stated decision, not an accident of which recorder method was called.

findings.title: Duplicate detection is adjacency-only against `last_steps[-1]`, and `last_steps` carries across task boundaries
findings.detail: `guard_duplicate` reads `last = controller.state["last_steps"][-1:]` and returns None immediately unless `last[0]["action"] == act` (askme.py:3017-3022). So the ban is not permanent: an already-succeeded command re-executes normally if ANY other action intervenes. Precise answer to 'can a task whose criterion is an already-succeeded command ever be satisfied without re-executing it?' — it can be satisfied by re-executing it (non-adjacently), or by the model emitting `done` after reading the corrective note 'Already ran successfully — use the earlier output. Take the next action, or emit done/fail.' (askme.py:3138-3141). What it cannot do is be satisfied from the record alone. Separately, `_execute_tasks` seeds each task with the previous task's final step (`prev_last = self.state["last_steps"][-1:]`, askme.py:4281, applied at 4343), so a new task's very FIRST action can be classified a duplicate of the previous task's last step when the args match exactly — the classic verify-only replan shape.
findings.next_step: State the mechanism precisely in public: a 2-strike adjacency counter, not a permanent ban. Overclaiming 'the harness refuses to re-run successful commands' would be wrong.

findings.title: Every listed coverage gap sits inside the completion / obligation / validation machinery
findings.detail: Mapping the parent's uncovered ranges: askme.py 1483->1488 and 1494-1500 are `_extract_error_type`'s prefix parse and heuristic fallbacks — including line 1498 `return "stuck_loop", err`, the fallback classification of the very error string this whole failure mode produces (live errors already carry the `[stuck_loop]` prefix, so the fallback is effectively dead). 1551 is the `continue` when `_mutation_target_key` returns None inside `_unresolved_incomplete_writes` — the incomplete-write completion blocker. 1576-1583 is the non-dict/legacy branch and the `recovery_arg` fallbacks of the incomplete-write display helper; 1599 is `_next_pending_empty`'s 'all obligations allow append' fallback; 1674-1678 is `_pending_append_targets`' legacy `append_target` handling — all three feed the `[incomplete_write] ... completion refused` path at askme.py:4288-4296. 2172-2208 is `_should_validate`'s decision branches plus the head of `_deterministic_check` (pending_empty_writes, unresolved truncated writes, empty-file check). 2248-2272 is `_validate_completion`'s deterministic-False rejection and the evidence block it hands the validator. 3607-3632 is `WriteObligations`' truncated-write `pending_empty_writes` bookkeeping. So: yes, all of them — the aggregate 96.61% branch coverage conceals that the code deciding 'is this run complete' is the least-exercised region in the two runtime files.
findings.next_step: Before publishing a coverage number, add targeted tests for `_should_validate`, `_deterministic_check`, and the incomplete-write recovery-arg fallbacks; or state publicly that the headline figure is aggregate and name this region as thinner.

findings.title: Docs disclose the failure class honestly, but two PERFORMANCE.md passages describe removed auto-done behavior
findings.detail: The honest disclosure is real and citable: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:345 names 'Done-emission loops on QAT weights (local, observed 2026-08-03)' — 'the model completes all steps correctly, then re-emits duplicate successful actions ... until the step budget exhausts — 2 of 5 E23 bench pytest failures, always with a correct deliverable on disk' — and docs/PERFORMANCE.md:179 repeats it; docs/PERFORMANCE.md:45 says the agent 'completed the work — compile fixed, binary built and ran — then exhausted'. Both correctly say these runs 'correctly end exhausted' per issue #68 and point at `AGENT_STEP_POLICY=lifecycle` as the untested lever. However docs/PERFORMANCE.md:576 says 'task 2 auto-done via duplicate guard' and the table at docs/PERFORMANCE.md:679-681 shows 'Write main.c loop (same content) | ... | 1 write → auto-done'. The current code does the opposite: askme.py:3115-3118 states 'Repetition is never completion evidence (issue #68): the duplicate is suppressed as a no-op once ... task acceptance still requires an explicit done.' Those are dated entries and legitimate history, but a blog post quoting that table would describe behavior the code no longer has.
findings.next_step: Do not edit the frozen entries; when quoting them publicly, date-stamp them and add a one-line 'superseded by issue #68' pointer so no reader infers current auto-done behavior.

findings.title: The documented remedy (`AGENT_STEP_POLICY=lifecycle`) is stricter about `done`, not looser — it is not obviously the fix
findings.detail: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:345 and docs/PERFORMANCE.md:179 both point at the lifecycle arm as 'the sanctioned lever to evaluate against this class'. But `LifecycleStepPolicy.guard_done` (askme.py:3387-3407) REFUSES `done` while `needs_verification` is set, emitting skip reason `lifecycle_unverified_done`; `needs_verification` is cleared only by a successful shell inside `note_result` (askme.py:3452-3454), which is called only from `_execute_step` (askme.py:4586) — never for a suppressed duplicate. It also refuses deterministic auto-completion (askme.py:3465-3468) and skips same-target rewrites (3409-3437, bumping the shared `dup_skip_count`). Direct adjacency deadlock is not trivially reachable (a write is always followed by an executable shell, since the guard only compares against the immediately previous step), but the arm strictly adds ways to refuse `done` on top of the guards that already cause exhaustion. Recommending it publicly as the remedy is not yet evidence-backed.
findings.next_step: Before the blog post repeats the lifecycle recommendation, run a matched heuristic-vs-lifecycle comparison on the `multi_step_build` / `create_and_read_file` tasks under a registered protocol, or soften the claim to 'a candidate lever we have not yet measured'.

stale_or_wrong: docs/PERFORMANCE.md:576 — 'task 2 auto-done via duplicate guard' describes pre-issue-#68 behavior; askme.py:3113-3118 now states repetition is never completion evidence and acceptance still requires an explicit done.

docs/PERFORMANCE.md:679-681 — the before/after table row 'Write main.c loop (same content) | 5 writes → exhausted steps → replan | 1 write → auto-done' advertises an auto-done that the current duplicate guard does not perform (askme.py:3106-3112 only escalates thinking).
Any public phrasing that a run 'fails' — the code has no failed run status; non-completing runs are `exhausted` (askme.py:2927, 3840-3856, 4751-4752).

Any public phrasing that the harness 'verifies completion' — in the default heuristic arm it verifies only that no incomplete-write obligation is open and then trusts the model's `done` (askme.py:4560-4568, 2997-2999).
not_checked: Issue #95's actual text — the `gh` CLI is not installed in this container (`gh: command not found`) and I did not spend budget on the GitHub MCP tools; all #95 grounding here comes from code and frozen records, not the issue body.

The berkeley-protocol cell failures in scheduled run 135 (medium/test_fix_python_syntax_error on google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it and qwen/qwen3.6-27b) — I did not open those logs, so I cannot say whether they share this mechanism or are a different (e.g. planner/parse) failure.
actions.py — I only grepped it; the guards, recorder, obligations, completion policy and controller all live in askme.py, so no actions.py line is cited as load-bearing here.

The executor prompt text that steers the model toward emitting `done` (get_step / prompt construction) — not read, so I cannot say how strongly the model is instructed to finish after a duplicate note.
Whether any live run has actually hit the cross-guard `dup_skip_count` priming case (finding 6) — the frozen records I sampled show single-guard sequences only.
Live behavior of AGENT_STEP_POLICY=lifecycle — no live or paid model calls were made in this audit.
blog_story_material: The single best worked example in the repo: tests/bench_records/2026-08-03/12b_easy/test_multi_step_build_trial1.jsonl — a local run that writes main.c, compiles and runs it successfully, then re-issues the same successful `cc -o main main.c` twice, gets `duplicate_shell` then `stuck_shell_repeat`, replans to `gcc`, repeats the identical cycle, and ends `run_end status=exhausted`. Correct binary on disk, run reported as exhausted. Frozen, dated, self-contained.

A genuinely interesting design tension to write about honestly: issue #68 removed the old 'latest shell succeeded, call it complete' reconciliation because it manufactured false successes that contaminated evaluation. That was the right call. But removing it left no receipt-backed acceptance at all, so the pendulum sits at 'only the model's word counts'. The missing middle — a verification ledger that accepts a task when a recorded, in-run receipt proves its criterion held — is a clean, unbuilt idea.

The asymmetry that a repeated harmless read ends the attempt (askme.py:3170-3179) while a repeated wasteful write only escalates thinking (askme.py:3106-3112) is a concrete, checkable example of how loop-protection heuristics drift out of proportion to the risk they guard.

Small models fail at emitting a terminal token, not at the work. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:345 and docs/PERFORMANCE.md:179 already document this as the dominant local failure class on E4B QAT Q4_0 — 'always with a correct deliverable on disk'. That is a much more interesting story than a capability claim, and it is already backed by retained records.

The honest coverage caveat: 96.61% branch coverage overall, yet `_should_validate`, `_deterministic_check`, the validator evidence builder and the incomplete-write recovery fallbacks are all in the uncovered set — i.e. the least-tested code is the code that decides whether a run succeeded. Saying that out loud is more credible than the headline number.

summary: Issue #94's central claim is CONFIRMED in code, on every one of its five mechanism links, and I found one additional fact that strengthens it: `content_truncated` is in `_RESERVED_ACTION_FIELDS` (actions.py:848-855), so even a model that tried to declare truncation is schema-rejected. The only remaining producer of `content_truncated=True` anywhere in the runtime is askme.py:4498-4502, a seam whose own comment labels it as serving "patched/injected clients." However, this is NOT undocumented dead code: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:200-203 already states verbatim that the intake and chunked-append recovery "remain for the structured run API and injected clients, but the wire decoder no longer produces partial content." The stale artifact is CLAUDE.md:153-160, whose "Truncation and observation integrity" invariant is written as unconditional live behavior with no such caveat — that is the file a post-talk reader opens first. Separately, the JSON-transport removal in 5e59dd6 is a genuinely clean migration: sentinel framing is gone with negative regression tests, `ACTION_TRANSPORT="tools"` is a deliberately retained hash-log constant, and `_decode_action_reply` is still live (planner/replan/validation are still plain JSON, not actions) — so "leftover dead JSON code" is largely not a real finding. Two things do need disclosure before a public post: the #41 C-header compile-repair heuristic is WIRED and ON BY DEFAULT (askme.py:418), so it is a confound in any C-task result; and the 512-token write cap does NOT bind by default — the shipped default profile is `generic-feature-scale-v1` at 8192 write tokens, with 512 living only in the opt-in `legacy-e4b-m1-16k-v1` local profile. Code health is otherwise a strong public signal: zero TODO/FIXME/XXX/HACK comments in 6051 lines of runtime code, offset by a 224-line `__init__` and a 198-line `guard_duplicate`. Finally, #94's own live-impact evidence is not retained on main.

findings.title: Issue #94 confirmed in code: no wire producer of incomplete_write exists after the tools-only migration
findings.detail: Verified every link of #94's mechanism chain independently. (1) `_decode_tool_call_reply` (askme.py:1085-1125) is the sole executor-action decoder; on a payload cut at the token budget, `json.loads(raw_arguments)` raises and line 1117 raises `_tool_reply_error("tool call arguments are not valid JSON (truncated)")` — the entire envelope, content included, is discarded. (2) Its success path at line 1125 always constructs a DEFAULT `ActionTransport()`; there is no call site anywhere that builds `ActionTransport(content_truncated=True)` from a model reply. (3) `ctx.truncated_write = act == "write" and ctx.transport.content_truncated` (askme.py:3537) is therefore permanently False in a real run. (4) So `StepReceipt.executed(..., truncated_write=...)` never sets `_truncated_write` (actions.py:1058-1059) and `_unresolved_incomplete_writes` (askme.py:1539) never finds anything. NEW EVIDENCE #94 does not cite: `_RESERVED_ACTION_FIELDS = frozenset({"content_truncated", "finish_reason", "transport", "truncated_write"})` (actions.py:848-855) means a model that emitted `content_truncated` in its tool arguments is rejected by `parse_action_envelope`, closing the last theoretical wire path. The only surviving producer is askme.py:4498-4502, reachable only when the decoded action is a plain dict rather than a `DecodedAction` — i.e. an injected client.
evidence: askme.py:1085-1125 (_decode_tool_call_reply; raise at 1117, `return _accept_or_raise(envelope, cleaned, ActionTransport())` at 1125)
findings.next_step: Decide #94 explicitly (salvage the longest valid prefix, or formally retire the path) BEFORE the blog post, because CLAUDE.md currently advertises the recovery half of the invariant as live.

findings.title: CLAUDE.md's 'Truncation and observation integrity' invariant is the stale artifact, not ARCHITECTURE.md
findings.detail: This is the key nuance a synthesis step must not get wrong. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md is HONEST and current: its Interface revision 6 section (lines 186-206) states verbatim "The `content_truncated` intake, incomplete-write obligations, and chunked-append recovery remain for the structured run API and injected clients, but the wire decoder no longer produces partial content." It was updated in the removal commit itself (`git log -1 -- docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` -> 5e59dd6). By contrast CLAUDE.md:153-160 states "A partial/truncated mutation is `incomplete_write`, never a complete or merely unvalidated artifact. Preserve an actionable resume boundary and target" with no caveat, as an unconditional engineering invariant. A reader arriving from the talk reads CLAUDE.md/README first and will conclude the harness commits-and-resumes partial writes from live models. It does not. Likewise tests/workflows/PROTOCOL.md:74-82 describes the sentinel transport and resume-anchor recovery, but that text is explicitly scoped as 'revision-3 results' in a frozen protocol, so it is legitimately historical and should NOT be counted as stale.
evidence: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:200-203 ("but the wire decoder no longer produces partial content")
tests/workflows/PROTOCOL.md:74-82 (correctly scoped as revision-3, not stale)
findings.next_step: Add the ARCHITECTURE.md caveat sentence to the CLAUDE.md invariant, or resolve #94 so the invariant becomes true again.

findings.title: The #41 C-header compile-repair heuristic is wired and ON BY DEFAULT — a confound in any public C-task claim
findings.detail: `COMPILE_REPAIR_ENABLED = os.environ.get("AGENT_COMPILE_REPAIR", "1") == "1"` (askme.py:418) — default ON. It is fully wired end to end: `RunConfig.compile_repair` (askme.py:2820, read from env at 2851), resolved at 3988-3989, hash-logged into the run config payload at 4069, and dispatched at 4623-4624 via `_compile_repair_action(result.output, self.working_dir, action.get("arg", ""), enabled=self.compile_repair)`. The rule body is a hard-coded pattern table `_COMPILE_REPAIR_PATTERNS` (askme.py:2320-2341) that injects literal `#include <stdio.h>` and `#include <string.h>` on matching compile errors. The boundary conversion CLAUDE.md describes did land (it proposes a normal action through the executor), but the retain-vs-remove decision is still open per the roadmap. Practical consequence: every shipped run and every retained bench record ran with this heuristic ENABLED, so a public claim that a small local model 'fixed the C compile error' is partly a claim about a hardcoded lookup table.
findings.next_step: Disclose the default-on state in any public C-task narrative, or run the preregistered #41 off-arm at a pinned revision before citing C results.

findings.title: The 512-token write cap is opt-in legacy, not the shipped default — do not describe it as 'the' harness constraint
findings.detail: `_default_capability_profile()` (askme.py:204-206) returns `_GENERAL_PROFILE` = `generic-feature-scale-v1` with `step_tokens=4096, step_write_tokens=8192` (askme.py:183-187). The 512-token write cap exists ONLY in `_LEGACY_E4B_PROFILE` = `legacy-e4b-m1-16k-v1` (askme.py:175-182): `step_tokens=256, step_write_tokens=512, reasoning_token_floors=(512,512,768), context_window=16384, server_slots=1`. It binds only when explicitly selected via `LLM_CAPABILITY_PROFILE` (askme.py:209-211) or `--capability-profile` (askme.py:4792-4794). The whole vector is frozen and hash-logged via `capabilities.describe()` into the run config (askme.py:159-172, 4037-4053), which is a genuinely good reproducibility story. blog_story_material: The strongest honest story in this subsystem: removing a custom transport silently orphaned an invariant. The sentinel-framed <<<CONTENT/CONTENT>>> transport existed to solve JSON-string escaping AND to make truncation recoverable — when the closing sentinel was missing, the harness committed the complete lines that arrived and handed the model a resume anchor. Native tool calls solved the escaping problem cleanly (arguments carry strings unescaped) but reintroduced all-or-nothing truncation: a payload cut mid-string is unparseable JSON, so the whole write is discarded. One failure mode was traded for another, and an entire CLAUDE.md invariant section quietly lost its producer. That is a specific, technically credible, self-critical anecdote about agent-harness design — and the repo's own ARCHITECTURE.md documented it accurately (askme.py:1117 / docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:200-203, issue #94).

The capability-profile mechanism is a genuinely good reproducibility idea worth explaining: one named profile freezes the entire budget vector (step/write/planner/replan/validation tokens, reasoning floors, context window, server slots) and describe() feeds it into a hash-logged run config, so two runs with different budgets can never be silently compared. legacy-e4b-m1-16k-v1 (256/512, 16k ctx, 1 slot) versus generic-feature-scale-v1 (4096/8192) makes the local-vs-hosted distinction a first-class, machine-checkable object rather than a caption. askme.py:120-206, 4037-4057.
Zero TODO/FIXME/XXX/HACK comments across 6051 lines of runtime code (askme.py + actions.py). Small, verifiable, and unusual — a fair thing to point at when inviting people to read the source.

A concrete small-model engineering detail with a dated cause: tool_choice is 'auto' and deliberately never 'required', because grammar-forced tool choice corrupted native Gemma 4 string delimiters into argument text on llama.cpp b9618's PEG parser in the 2026-08-04 smoke run. That is the kind of specific, traceable local-inference war story the talk audience came for. askme.py:928-932.

The selected/executed/skipped step accounting is a nice framing for 'what an agent actually did versus what it proposed' — the 2026-07-31 Qwen canary selected 14 reads of which only 2 executed, and that gap is now a first-class run_end metric rather than something reconstructed from logs. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:208.

A caution to build into the post rather than a claim: the harness ships a hard-coded C-header repair table (#include <stdio.h> / <string.h>) that is ON by default and fires on compile errors. Being upfront that a deterministic heuristic sits behind some C fixes — and that the ablation deciding its fate is still open (issue #41) — is more credible than letting a reader discover askme.py:2320-2341 themselves.

summary: AskMe's evidence base is unusually strong on process discipline and unusually thin on current-truth numbers. Every outcome-bearing claim traces to a dated PERFORMANCE.md entry plus retained raw records (tests/bench_records/2026-08-03/, tests/bench_records/2026-08-04/, tests/featurebench/results/, talks/berkeley-agentic-ai-summit-2026/evals/), and the repo consistently retains negatives, infrastructure-corrupted runs, provenance defects, and self-corrections rather than deleting them — that retention record is the single most credible thing in the repository and the best blog material. The E-series registry runs E01-E25 only; there is no E26 or E27, so any plan referencing them is referencing nothing. E23 (2026-08-03, local E4B QAT Q4_0) and E25 (2026-08-04, json-vs-tools transport A/B) are the only two local benches with retained records; E21 has been marked "running" since 2026-08-02 with wiring landed but zero live cells, and E22 (the #41 compile-repair ablation) is an explicitly unregistered draft. The known stale claim is confirmed: docs/gemma4-setup.md:21 still advertises "E23 full bench: hard 9/9" while docs/PERFORMANCE.md:80-83 and tests/bench_records/2026-08-04/README.md both record that neither E25 arm reproduced it and that the reference "should not be cited as current until re-benched"; the same superseded framing survives in docs/EXPERIMENTS.md:66, :115 and :416, and the retraction propagated to none of them. The bigger public-facing risk is not stale local numbers but the talk's headline hosted result: the 7/8-accepted matrix (2026-07-10, commit 04033b47, one trial per cell) includes medium/test_fix_python_syntax_error passing on both google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it and qwen/qwen3.6-27b, and that exact cell is what failed on both models in scheduled LLM Tests runs 132-135 against byte-identical askme.py/actions.py. The cheapest, highest-value next measurement is a multi-trial re-run of the two Berkeley protocol cells (~$0.20) to convert a one-shot headline into a variance-bearing statement before publication.

findings.detail: Issue #95 (opened 2026-08-30, state open) reports that on the seeded-repair cell test_webapp_fix_failing_health_check, 20/20 runs produced a successful edit, 20/20 passed python3 test_app.py in-run, held-out acceptance passed on all checked runs, yet only 9/20 were recorded complete and 11/20 exhausted; `done` was emitted zero times in all 20 runs. findings.title: No GitHub-hosted macOS runner can reproduce the M1 16 GB reference; the arithmetic rules out all three
findings.detail: PR #96's macos.yml states the sizing directly in its header comment: "macos-26  M1, 3 vCPU, 7 GB — free/unlimited on public repos; macos-26-xlarge  M2 Pro, 5 vCPU, 14 GB — billed per-minute, always; macos-26-large  Intel, 12 vCPU, 30 GB — not Apple Silicon, no Metal". Memory need for the reference: 5.15 GB of weights resident under -ngl 99 (unified memory), plus a 16384-token q4_0 K+V cache with --swa-full (which deliberately disables the sliding-window KV savings), plus OS and Python. Verdict per runner: macos-26 (7 GB) NO — 5.15 GB of weights leaves under ~1.5 GB for KV, OS and the harness; it would swap or be OOM-killed, and PR #96 explicitly gates against this. macos-26-large (30 GB) NO for the purpose — it is Intel, so there is no Metal backend at all and -ngl 99 is meaningless; whatever it measured would be CPU inference, not the reference deployment. macos-26-xlarge (14 GB, M2 Pro) is the only candidate that holds the model, and it is still 2 GB below the 16 GB reference machine and a different chip generation. So the honest public statement is: the local M1 result is not reproducible on GitHub-hosted CI, and PR #96 says so in its own comment header ("No lane here produces performance evidence... timings from this workflow must never be written into docs/PERFORMANCE.md"). What PR #96's llama-reference lane provides instead is a FUNCTIONAL parity check on a runner label you supply: inputs are runner (default macos-26-xlarge), min_memory_gb (default "12"; set 16 to demand true parity), model_repo (default google/gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf), model_file (default gemma-4-E4B_q4_0-it.gguf), model_revision (default main), and suite (easy/medium/hard). tests/ci_local_gate.py hardware runs the memory floor check BEFORE the 5.15 GB download so an undersized runner fails fast rather than looking like an agent-loop bug.

findings.title: OpenRouter wiring, precisely: one workflow, one environment, two jobs, four cells, two pinned dated snapshots, one identity gate
findings.detail: Workflow: .github/workflows/llm.yml (name "LLM Tests"). Credential: environment secret OPENROUTER_API_KEY, scoped to the GitHub deployment environment named "Openrouter" (llm.yml:15-16, :69, :130); both jobs declare `environment: Openrouter`. Access guard (llm.yml:67 and :128, identical): the job runs only if the event is not a pull_request, OR the PR head repo equals the base repo AND the PR carries the 'llm-tests' label — so a fork PR is rejected before the credential is ever in scope, consistent with CLAUDE.md's credential rules. Cells: 2 models x 2 tasks = 4. Models default (llm.yml:33, :154) to `google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it=google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it-20260403,qwen/qwen3.6-27b=qwen/qwen3.6-27b-20260422` — requested=expected-served syntax with an optional @low/@medium/@high effort suffix. findings.title: The 'CI design defect, not code regression' claim is SUPPORTED by the config — with one correction: the reds are cell-correlated, not random
findings.detail: Supported by the actual config. Trials: TRIALS defaults to "1" (llm.yml:41, :156) and is passed straight through as --trials to both bench_harness invocations (llm.yml:192, :199). Retries: grep for retry/continue-on-error/max-attempts in llm.yml returns ZERO matches — no step retries, no job retries, no re-roll. Pass rule: tests/ci_llm_gate.py:336, `passed = total > 0 and pytest_passed == total and agent_complete == total` — a cell is green only if EVERY trial is both a pytest pass and an agent completion, so at trials=1 a single non-claiming run reds the cell. Strictness asymmetry: --advisory-cell-failures is applied only when GITHUB_EVENT_NAME == "push" (llm.yml:212-214); scheduled runs, manual dispatches and PRs are STRICT. So the identical code that is advisory-green on a main push is hard-red on Monday's cron. That is exactly the shape of runs 132-135 (scheduled) vs run 130. Combined with issue #95's measured 11/20 (55%) claim-failure rate on work that was correct 20/20 and independently accepted, a 4-cell all-must-pass n=1 gate has a low ceiling on green even with zero regressions. CORRECTION to the claim: this is not "model variance." Run 135's two protocol failures were the SAME cell (medium/test_fix_python_syntax_error) on BOTH google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it and qwen/qwen3.6-27b, while hard/test_replan_build_with_dependency passed on both — a correlated, task-specific failure, not a random draw. And the smoke failure was status "exhausted" with "[stuck_loop] read ...: same file read repeatedly", which is the same mechanism family issue #95 documents ([stuck_loop] guard suppresses a redundant re-check, the task cannot be satisfied, the run exhausts despite finished work). So the accurate public sentence is: the gate design (n=1, no retries, all-cells-must-pass, strict on schedule) makes it maximally sensitive, and what it is sensitive TO is a real, reproducible completion-claiming defect (#95) rather than a change in askme.py or actions.py — git diff eee3fb7 fcd5bc0 leaves both runtime files byte-identical.

Local is dense E4B (5.15 GB, Dense PLE + iSWA); the only Gemma 4 MoE is 26B-A4B, which does not fit 16 GB and only ever ran hosted. If the person who built the setup can conflate them in one sentence, so will every reader. This is a genuinely useful paragraph about why the repo writes 'requested=expected-served' cells and hashes the GGUF it loaded.

'The CI went red and nothing changed' — a clean, verifiable story: four consecutive scheduled LLM Tests runs (132-135) failed on fcd5bc0, the last green was run 130 on eee3fb7, and git diff between them touches only docs and bench records; askme.py and actions.py are byte-identical. The reds came from a single-trial, no-retry, all-cells-must-pass live gate (tests/ci_llm_gate.py:336) sampling a real completion-claiming defect. Good material for 'how do you build CI around a stochastic system'.

Issue #95 is the strongest and most honest number in the repo: on a task the agent solves 20/20 with independently accepted, held-out-verified repairs, the harness records 11/20 runs as 'exhausted' because it never claims the work. 'The model did the job every time and told us so about half the time' is a memorable, defensible line — and it is a harness bug, not a model-capability result, which is a distinction most agent posts get wrong.

The [stuck_loop] irony: the guard that exists to stop repetition-as-acceptance ('re-running a passing test is not progress') is what strands a finished run — the replanner emits a verify-only task, the guard suppresses the verification because it already succeeded, the task cannot be satisfied, and the run burns its budget. Two invariants that are individually correct compose into a failure mode. Run 135's smoke failure was literally '[stuck_loop] read ...: same file read repeatedly' -> status exhausted.

'You cannot rent your laptop': GitHub offers M1/7 GB free, M2 Pro/14 GB billed, and Intel/30 GB with no Metal. None of them is a 16 GB M1. The silent-skip hole, twice closed: conftest.py skips local suites when :8080 is absent and skips OpenRouter suites without the opt-in, so a broken backend would read as a green run. Both workflows defend against it explicitly — llm.yml asserts llm-logs/smoke.jsonl is non-empty ('Assert the suite really ran (no silent skips)'), and macos.yml gates on a preflight before the advisory probe. 'A skipped integration suite is not evidence that a backend works' is already in CLAUDE.md and is enforced in YAML.

Moving weights under a fixed name: Google republished every Gemma 4 checkpoint on 2026-07-15/16 under identical filenames. That is why macos.yml records x-repo-commit and a sha256 of the actual GGUF into the job summary and warns when model_revision=main. Concrete, unglamorous provenance engineering that most model-eval posts skip.

summary: The deterministic suite is genuinely strong in the places that matter most for a public release: 1208 passed / 24 skipped in ~37s, branch coverage 96.6% against a 90% gate, strict pytest settings (`filterwarnings=["error"]`, `xfail_strict=true`, `--strict-markers --strict-config`), and real, reachable coverage of the two invariants an outside reader is most likely to probe — observation-integrity truncation reasons for read/search/tree, and credential exclusion from results, events, config hashes, and CI workflows. Only 1 of ~1232 collected cases lacks a real assertion path, and that one is a false positive (it calls an asserting helper). The two credibility problems are structural, not cosmetic. First, all 24 skips are live-backend tests and their skip reason string conflates "you never opted in" with "the backend was down", so "1208 passed" is not and cannot be presented as evidence that either the local llama-server or the OpenRouter path works — exactly the trap CLAUDE.md warns about. Second, and worse for a public repo: issue #94's claim is independently confirmed here. `content_truncated=True` is never set by any live decode path (`_accept_or_raise` is called from askme.py:1062, 1069, 1125 and never with a truthy transport), so `incomplete_write`, resume-anchor recovery, and the run-wide incomplete-artifact obligation are reachable only through the injection seam at askme.py:4498-4504. Roughly 38 assertions across `TestTruncatedWriteContinuation` and neighbors drive that machinery by putting a literal `"content_truncated": True` key into a mocked `ask_llm` reply — a key the real decoder rejects. The suite simultaneously pins the opposite contract on the live path (`tests/test_agent_tool_transport.py:253`), so two green suites encode contradictory behavior and the gap is invisible. Separately, the repo's own documented commands do not run on a stock machine (`required-version = "==0.12.1"` is an exact pin), one legacy test burns 30.15s of the 36.67s suite runtime on a real `sleep 60`, issue #80's monkeypatch debt has grown from 487 to 490 sites across 15 files, and the 90% coverage gate covers only `askme.py`/`actions.py` — the evaluator and benchmark harness that produce the public evidence are outside it.

findings.title: incomplete_write / resume-anchor tests exercise a dead code path via the injection seam only — confirmed independently of issue #94
findings.detail:
Issue #94's central claim is verified from the code here, not taken on trust. `ActionTransport(content_truncated=True)` is constructed at exactly one place in askme.py — line 4502, inside the explicitly-labelled legacy compatibility branch whose own comment says 'the real model decoder rejects the same key and returns DecodedAction instead' (askme.py:4494-4504). Every live decode call site passes a default transport: askme.py:1062 `_accept_or_raise(parsed, text)`, :1069 `_accept_or_raise(repaired, text)`, and the tools-transport path :1125 `_accept_or_raise(envelope, cleaned, ActionTransport())`. Since ACTION_TRANSPORT = 'tools' (askme.py:218) is the only transport post-#92 and the JSON-envelope sentinel prompt was removed (askme.py:587-588), `ctx.truncated_write = act == "write" and ctx.transport.content_truncated` (askme.py:3537) is always False in a real run, so `_unresolved_incomplete_writes` (askme.py:1539) never finds anything and `_completion_blocker` (askme.py:1645) never fires for truncation.

Every test that drives this machinery injects the state directly. `tests/test_agent_actions.py:1128 class TestTruncatedWriteContinuation` opens with `@patch("askme.ask_llm")` and a `side_effect` list whose second element is a raw dict: `{"action": "write", "arg": "impl.py", "content": "line1\nline2\nline3 par", "content_truncated": True}` (lines 1132-1141). That literal key is the injection seam — a model can never produce it. The same construction repeats at test_agent_actions.py lines 1175, 1214, 1250, 1277, 1301, 1332, 1764, 1948, 1980, 2012, 2053, 2059, 2115, 2122, 2165, 2209, 2219 and more (38 `content_truncated` occurrences in that one file). The seven tests in TestTruncatedWriteContinuation (test_partial_lines_written_then_append_completes, test_truncated_write_output_carries_resume_anchor, test_empty_truncated_write_not_told_to_append, test_empty_truncated_append_chunk_stays_append, test_line_boundary_truncation_drops_nothing, test_no_complete_line_skips_dispatch, test_reemitted_truncated_prefix_is_clean_restart) plus the symlink-alias obligation family (test_agent_actions.py:1937-2300) all depend on it. `tests/test_agent_step_policy.py`, `tests/test_agent_completion_gates.py`, and `tests/test_agent_run_state.py` reference `incomplete_write` a further 7 times, likewise from constructed state.

The damning part is that the suite ALSO pins the contradictory live behavior, in green, in a different file: `tests/test_agent_tool_transport.py:253 test_exhausted_truncated_arguments_raise_response_truncated` feeds a genuinely cut tool-call payload (`'{"arg": "big.py", "content": "line one\\nline tw'`, finish_reason='length') and asserts `pytest.raises(json.JSONDecodeError, match="truncated")` with `response_truncated is True` — i.e. the whole write, content included, is discarded. So one suite certifies 'partial write is committed and resumed' and another certifies 'partial write is thrown away', and both pass.

findings.title: All 24 skips are live-backend tests, and the skip reason cannot distinguish 'not opted in' from 'backend down'
findings.detail:
Full breakdown from `pytest tests/ -q -rs`. Group A — local llama-server on :8080, reason string 'live LLM tests not enabled or llama-server not running on :8080', 13 tests: tests/test_agent_integration.py lines 31, 40, 46, 62, 80, 100, 117, 134, 152, 366, 385, 411 and tests/test_agent_planning.py:424. Group B — OpenRouter, reason 'live LLM tests not enabled or OpenRouter API not available', 11 tests: tests/test_agent_integration.py lines 187, 195, 200, 214, 229, 246, 262, 278, 292, 318, 337. There is no third group; every skip is backend-gated, none are platform or dependency skips.

The gating logic (tests/conftest.py:71-82) is `pytest.mark.skipif(not live_llm_enabled or not _llm_available(), reason=...)`. Two separate conditions collapse into one reason string. Concretely: a contributor who sets ASKME_RUN_LIVE_LLM_TESTS=1 but has no llama-server running gets a skip line byte-identical to a contributor who never opted in. Nothing in the run output — not the reason, not a marker, not the count — distinguishes 'the backend was never asked' from 'the backend was asked and was unreachable'. For a project whose CLAUDE.md states 'A skipped integration suite is not evidence that a backend works', the harness cannot itself tell the two apart.

What IS defensible and worth saying: the short-circuit in `not live_llm_enabled or not _openrouter_available()` means Python never evaluates the probe when the env var is absent, so the default suite genuinely makes zero network calls and reads no credential — the network-free/credential-free claim in CLAUDE.md holds.

findings.title: The 90% coverage gate covers only askme.py and actions.py — the evidence-producing infrastructure is outside it
findings.detail:
pyproject.toml [tool.coverage.run] sets `source = ["askme", "actions"]` with branch = true, and [tool.coverage.report] sets fail_under = 90. ci.yml:73-74 passes `--cov=askme --cov=actions` and runs coverage only on the Python 3.14 matrix leg (ci.yml:69, 81, 89). So the modules that produce the project's public evidence — tests/workflow_eval.py (the native semantic workflow evaluator), tests/bench_harness.py, tests/featurebench/askme_adapter.py, tests/featurebench/canary_audit.py, tests/ci_llm_gate.py — carry no coverage floor at all. They are type-checked (pyproject.toml [tool.ty.src] include lists all five) and they do have their own test files, but a regression in the evaluator or the canary audit cannot fail the coverage gate. For a project whose credibility rests on 'claims trace to frozen records', the record-producing code is the code least protected by the headline number.

The 96.61% figure is therefore accurate but narrower than a reader will assume: it describes the two runtime modules, not the harness as a whole.

findings.title: Observation-integrity truncation coverage is real, reachable, and defensible to cite publicly
findings.detail:
This is the counterweight to the incomplete_write finding and is worth stating in the blog post because it is the invariant most likely to be probed. Unlike the truncation-recovery family, the read/search/tree truncation tests call the production `execute(...)` against real files on disk and assert the user-visible contract. tests/test_agent_actions.py carries explicit `truncation_reasons` assertions for every documented cap: 'matches' (:272), 'snippets' (:291), 'files' (:300), 'chars' (:308, :438), 'unreadable' (:348), 'entries' (:407), 'depth' (:428), 'walk_errors' (:463) — and, critically, negative cases asserting `truncation_reasons == []` when no cap was hit (:285, :317, :415), which is what makes the positive assertions meaningful.

Continuation resume-reconstruction is likewise covered against reconstructed artifacts, not internal flags: test_window_header_and_continuation (:69), test_continuation_navigation_covers_whole_file (:80), test_last_window_has_no_continuation (:88), test_offset_past_eof (:95), test_long_single_line_reconstructs_exactly (:124), test_wide_multiline_pages_reconstruct_to_eof (:134), test_nondefault_limit_is_preserved_through_reconstruction (:144), test_stale_hash_rejects_continuation (:165), test_cursor_requires_valid_continuation_limit (:182). These match the CLAUDE.md invariant clause by clause ('long lines, wide multi-line windows, repeated continuation to EOF').

findings.title: Credential-exclusion invariants have genuine end-to-end coverage across runtime, CI, and the canary auditor
findings.detail: Also defensible to state publicly. The CLAUDE.md rule 'Never print, persist, upload, or copy API keys into fixtures, logs, artifacts, issues, or PR text' is backed by tests at four distinct layers: tests/test_agent_run_api.py:367 test_result_and_events_never_carry_the_api_key; tests/test_agent_run_config.py:460 test_credentials_never_reach_the_hash_or_metadata; tests/test_ci_workflows_contract.py:81 test_workflows_do_not_persist_checkout_credentials; tests/test_featurebench_adapter.py:71 and :116 (strict OpenRouter environment omits the credential; launcher scrubs the transient credential before agent actions); and tests/test_featurebench_canary_audit.py:895/:908/:923 including test_secret_scan_detects_value_split_across_streaming_chunks and test_missing_api_key_makes_leak_audit_invalid — the latter is the right shape, because it refuses to call the leak audit valid when it had no key to look for.

findings.title: No assertion-free or trivially-passing tests found — the one AST candidate is a false positive
findings.detail:
An AST scan of every `test_*` function in tests/test_*.py for functions containing zero ast.Assert nodes returned 44 hits. 43 of them are `pytest.raises`/`pytest.warns` with-block tests, which is the correct idiom (e.g. tests/test_agent_tool_transport.py:202-227, tests/test_agent_run_config.py:70-169). The single remaining candidate, tests/test_agent_integration.py:292 test_replan_multi_step_recovery, has no inline assert and no with-block — but it ends in `assert_file(tmp_path / "config.json", "SUCCESS")`, a module helper that does assert. So it can fail. There is no `assert True`, no bare `pass` test, and no xfail in the suite; xfail_strict = true and filterwarnings = ["error"] are set in pyproject.toml, so a warning is a failure and an unexpectedly-passing xfail would be an error. On the specific charge 'assertions that cannot fail', the repo is clean and this can be said publicly.

One residual caveat: tests/test_agent_actions.py contains 13 inline `pytest.skip("file/directory symlinks are unavailable")` guards (lines 61, 345, 1891, 1973, 2005, 2045, 2103, 2157, 2192, 2268, 2315, 2362, 2417). CI is ubuntu-only (ci.yml:18, 44), so they never trip there, but a contributor on a symlink-restricted Windows checkout silently loses the entire symlink-alias identity-normalization family with no signal beyond a higher skip count.

findings.detail: Walking the 'Engineering invariants' block against the suite: (a) Truncation and observation integrity — the observation half (bounded read/search/tree must not look complete) is covered and reachable; the mutation half ('A partial/truncated mutation is incomplete_write... Preserve an actionable resume boundary and target') is covered only through the injection seam and is unreachable in production, per the release-blocker finding above. (b) Continuations must resume at the first unread content, reconstructed without gaps or duplication — covered and reachable (test_agent_actions.py:80-182). (c) 'An explicit validator rejection cannot be erased by a later unavailable or malformed validator response. Require new successful mutation or shell evidence before a recheck' — covered: tests/test_agent_recovery.py:1477 test_validate_unavailable_is_complete_unverified, :1527 test_validate_recheck_capped_after_recovery, :1559 test_validate_recheck_requires_new_evidence. findings.title: conftest silently sources a repo-root .env into os.environ when live tests are opted in
findings.detail: tests/conftest.py:52-58: `_openrouter_available()` reads `<repo root>/.env` line by line and calls `os.environ.setdefault(k, v)` for every KEY=VALUE line before checking OPENROUTER_API_KEY. This only executes when ASKME_RUN_LIVE_LLM_TESTS=1 (short-circuit at conftest.py:78), so the default suite is unaffected and the network-free claim holds. But it means the opt-in path injects arbitrary key/value pairs from an untracked dotfile into the process environment of the whole test session, not just the OpenRouter credential, and it does so as a side effect of a function named `_openrouter_available`. For a public repo where readers will copy the live-test invocation, that is worth either narrowing to OPENROUTER_API_KEY or documenting.

blog_story_material: The strongest honest line about the suite is not the pass count, it is the shape: 1208 deterministic tests that make zero network calls and read zero credentials by default, with strict-markers, strict-config, xfail_strict and warnings-as-errors, plus 24 live-backend tests that are explicitly opt-in. The discipline of refusing to let a skipped integration suite count as backend evidence is itself the interesting claim — and it is enforced by the short-circuit in tests/conftest.py:78, not just by convention.

A genuinely good story for a post about building agent harnesses: the read/search/tree observation-integrity tests assert on `truncation_reasons` INCLUDING the negative cases (`== []` when no cap was hit, test_agent_actions.py:285, 317, 415). Most projects only assert the positive. The negative assertions are what make 'a bounded result must not look complete' a real contract rather than a slogan.

The most valuable and most uncomfortable story here is the incomplete_write one, and it is worth telling deliberately rather than hiding: a transport migration (#92, JSON envelope -> native tool calls) silently orphaned an entire recovery subsystem, and ~50 green assertions kept covering it because they injected the state through a compatibility seam a model can no longer produce. Two suites in the same repo now certify opposite behaviors and both pass. That is a precise, reproducible case study in how test coverage can survive the death of the code it covers — far more interesting to a technical reader than a clean-repo claim, provided the post says what was done about it (#94 options 1 or 2).

Concrete detail with a good hook: one legacy test that runs a real `sleep 60` against a 30-second production timeout accounts for 30.15 of the suite's 36.67 seconds — 82% of the wall clock in 1 of 1232 cases, paid five times over in the CI matrix.

A candid note on refactor debt that will resonate with anyone who has extracted a module: 490 tests patch symbols through the `askme` module namespace, which works only because everything still lives in one file. The injectable seams were built (#37/#40) and closed; the suite never moved onto them (RunDependencies appears in 3 test files). That single fact is what blocks splitting askme.py — a good illustration that landing a seam and adopting a seam are different projects.

Worth being precise about scope when quoting 96.61% branch coverage: it measures askme.py and actions.py. The evaluator and benchmark harness that produce the frozen records are type-checked but carry no coverage floor. Saying so unprompted is more credible than the number alone.
